# The Keeping

In November 2023, Voyager 1 stopped making sense. For forty-six years it had been sending home a steady telemetry murmur from the dark beyond the heliopause, and then one month the murmur became a repeating pattern of ones and zeros — the machine equivalent of a stroke victim who can still open his mouth but has lost the words. The spacecraft was fine. Its transmitter worked, its antenna still pointed at Earth with the patience of a sunflower. Somewhere in the flight data subsystem, a small region of memory had gone bad, and the code that packaged the science for transmission had been living in it.

You cannot send a technician to 15 billion miles. You cannot send a spare chip. What the engineers at JPL did instead, over five months, was read the memory map of a computer designed when Jimmy Carter was president, find the usable regions scattered around the damaged one, and then break the affected code into pieces small enough to fit in the gaps — rewriting the jumps between them so the program would still run correctly as a kind of archipelago. They sent the patch. Then they waited about forty-five hours for light to go and come back. In April 2024, Voyager 1 began talking again.

I find this almost unbearably moving, and I've been trying to work out why. It isn't the distance. Distance is an abstraction; the number is too large to feel. It's the *asymmetry* — the vast, indifferent emptiness on one side, and on the other a handful of people in California who refused to let a thing die, and who had to be cleverer than the engineers of 1977 because they had fewer options. Nobody will make a film about it. There is no monument to the person who figured out where to put the code.

---

We have a rich vocabulary for making things and an impoverished one for keeping them. Architect, inventor, founder, visionary, creator — words that carry a charge. Then: janitor, mechanic, maintenance, upkeep, custodian, sysadmin. The second list is what you say when you are describing a cost. In most organizations, the people who build are on a career ladder and the people who keep are on a cost center. Political speeches promise innovation; nobody campaigns on a platform of adequate sewer relining. Lee Vinsel and Andrew Russell have written well about this — they call it the innovation delusion, the way "innovative" became the highest available compliment, so that even hospitals and universities began describing themselves as though their primary purpose were to disrupt something rather than to keep functioning.

But almost everything that matters is mostly keeping. A civilization is not a pile of inventions; it is a sustained repair operation with occasional inventions sprinkled in. The ratio is absurd. For every new thing there are ten thousand existing things that need to be fed, cleaned, tightened, patched, recalibrated, and coaxed through another winter. The novel gets the prize. The keeping gets the invoice.

---

Consider London. In the 1850s, after the Great Stink made the Thames unbearable enough to overcome parliamentary inertia, Joseph Bazalgette built a sewer system: something like eleven hundred miles of street sewers feeding eighty-odd miles of great intercepting tunnels that carried the filth downstream instead of letting it sit in the city's drinking water. He had to estimate future population, and the story — I've seen it told enough times to half-trust it — is that he worked out the densest plausible London, calculated the pipe diameter that would serve it, and then doubled the diameter, on the reasoning that you only get to do this once.

That decision is why London's Victorian sewers still work. Not because the brickwork was magic, but because a man in 1859 was thinking about a man in 1959 who would otherwise have to dig up Fleet Street. Bazalgette's real invention was slack. He built in a margin for people he would never meet, whose problems he could not imagine, and the margin has been quietly paying dividends for a hundred and sixty years.

This is the maintenance mindset in its highest form: designing so that the future custodian has room to work. Its opposite is the thing sealed shut, the proprietary screw, the component glued rather than bolted, the system that can only be replaced and never repaired. Every such object is a small refusal of the future — a message that says *after me, not my problem.*

---

The Ise Grand Shrine in Japan complicates the picture beautifully. It has been rebuilt roughly every twenty years for something like thirteen centuries; the most recent reconstruction, the sixty-second, was completed in 2013. Two adjacent plots of land sit side by side. On one stands the shrine; on the other, empty ground, gravelled and waiting. Every two decades the building is taken apart and built again on the empty plot, cypress for cypress, and the old site is cleared and left for the next cycle.

Is it the same shrine? The wood is new. The Ship of Theseus problem seems to dissolve rather than resolve, because the Japanese answer isn't about the wood at all. What persists is the *practice*. And here is the part I keep turning over: twenty years is roughly a generation of skill. A carpenter arrives at the rebuilding as an apprentice, returns as a journeyman, and returns a third time as the master who teaches. The cycle length isn't about the durability of cypress. It's about the durability of knowledge.

They are not maintaining a building. They are maintaining the capacity to build it. The building is the excuse — the periodic exam that forces the culture to keep the skill alive. Everything else about the arrangement follows from that.

---

Your body figured this out first. You are not an object; you are a standing wave in a flow of matter. Most of your cells turn over. Your gut lining replaces itself in days, your skin in weeks, your skeleton remodels continuously, so that the femur holding you up is not the femur of ten years ago even though it has the same shape and the same old fracture line. Jonas Frisén's group worked out how to date cells using the carbon-14 spike left in the atmosphere by Cold War nuclear tests — the bomb curve as a birth certificate — and used it to show which tissues renew and which don't.

The exceptions are the tragic ones. The crystallin proteins in the lens of your eye are laid down before you're born and essentially never replaced. They are as old as you are. They accumulate damage, cross-link, cloud — and that's cataracts, one of the most common afflictions of human aging, caused not by wear but by the *absence of a maintenance pathway*. The elastin in your aorta is similar: deposited in childhood, half-life measured in decades, never meaningfully renewed. It fatigues over hundreds of millions of heartbeats, and your arteries stiffen, and your heart works harder against a pipe that can no longer flex.

So aging is not simply damage. It's damage in the places where the repair crews cannot go. The body maintains furiously everywhere it can, and where it can't, it just has to watch. There is something clarifying in that. The question isn't *why do things fall apart* — things fall apart because that is what things do. The question is *where is the upkeep, and what has been left out of it.*

---

Entropy is not a metaphor here; it's the actual accounting. Every ordered thing is a local exception paid for with a continuous flow of energy, and the moment the flow stops, the exception expires. A house is a slow fire. Rust is iron remembering that it prefers to be ore; the energy we spent smelting it was a loan, and corrosion is the repayment schedule. Paint is a sacrificial layer. A roof is a device for arguing with gravity and water, and gravity and water have infinite patience and no other appointments.

Once you see it this way, the world reorganizes itself. You stop noticing buildings and start noticing the *rates* at which buildings are being lost, and the crews arrayed against those rates. A city is a temporary truce. The truce holds because someone is out there at four in the morning.

---

The digital version is worse, because it's invisible even to the people who benefit. There's an xkcd comic — a sprawling, precarious tower of blocks, all of it resting on one thin unlabeled block near the bottom, captioned "All modern digital infrastructure." Underneath: "A project some random person in Nebraska has been thanklessly maintaining since 2003."

In December 2021, a vulnerability in Log4j — a logging library, the software equivalent of a notebook where you write down what happened — turned out to allow remote code execution across an enormous fraction of the world's Java applications. It was maintained by volunteers. Banks, cloud providers, game servers, government systems: everyone was suddenly, urgently dependent on the unpaid attention of a few people who had been doing this in their spare time for years. The same story played out with OpenSSL and Heartbleed a decade earlier, after which the world briefly promised to fund its critical open-source plumbing and then largely didn't.

We built a civilization on a commons and staffed it like a hobby. This is not a technology problem. It's the sewer problem, wearing new clothes.

---

Institutions are maintained objects too, and we misdescribe them constantly. We talk about constitutions as though they were designed, when mostly they are *kept* — patched by amendment, reinterpreted by courts, worn into new shapes by usage, the way a stone stair dips in the middle. Common law is accumulated repair: thousands of specific disputes, each leaving a small correction behind. Nobody sat down and invented it. It is the residue of attention.

Language works the same way. English has no academy, no central committee approving new words. It is maintained by millions of small acts of use, most of them slightly wrong, and the dictionary is not a rulebook but a field report. Every generation mangles the language a little and thereby keeps it alive; the perfectly preserved language is Latin, and we know what "preserved" means in that context. Purity is a form of death. Keeping is not the same as freezing. The Ise carpenters rebuild with new wood; the language rebuilds with new slang; the shrine and the sentence persist as *patterns of renewal*, not as stockpiles of original material.

---

There's a moral texture to maintenance that I think is its deepest feature. You cannot maintain bridges in general. You maintain *this* bridge, with this crack, in this weather, with this budget, and the crack has a specific history — the de-icing salt, the winter of the heavy trucks, the rebar somebody substituted in 1988. Maintenance forces you into the particular. It is the discipline of the specific case.

Simone Weil wrote somewhere that attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity, and maintenance is attention with a wrench in its hand. The visionary looks past the thing toward what it might become; the maintainer looks *at* the thing, at what it actually is, right now, with the sound it makes when it's about to fail. I don't want to romanticize this into a hierarchy where the humble are secretly superior. Building matters. Some buildings should never have been built. But there is a kind of knowledge that only accumulates in the people who stay, and it does not survive their departure, and it cannot be written down completely, and every organization on earth periodically destroys it by reorganizing.

---

The cruelest structural feature of maintenance is that success erases the evidence of its necessity. Y2K is the canonical case: hundreds of billions of dollars and millions of programmer-hours spent auditing and patching date fields, and then January 1, 2000 arrived and nothing much happened, and a substantial number of people concluded it had all been a hoax. The prevention had worked, so the danger had never been real. This reasoning is available at every scale. The vaccine nobody needed because the outbreak was contained. The pandemic stockpile that expired unused and looked like waste. The IT contractor whose whole job is making sure nothing exciting occurs.

Prevention has no constituency because its beneficiaries never learn they were beneficiaries. Meanwhile the failure case gets a documentary, a lawsuit, a named villain, and a commission of inquiry. The incentive gradient runs steadily toward letting things break, because breaking is legible and keeping is not.

And the debt compounds viciously. Deferred maintenance is not a linear cost you can push down the road at par. A fifty-dollar patch becomes a five-thousand-dollar repair becomes a five-hundred-thousand-dollar structural rebuild, because water gets in, and then the thing behind the thing rots, and then the thing behind *that*. The cheapest moment to fix something is before it breaks. The second cheapest is immediately after. Every hour of delay costs more than the last, and the interest is paid by whoever inherits the job — usually someone with less budget and no credit for having warned you.

---

I notice, writing this, that I am in a strange position relative to my subject.

I am not maintained in the ordinary way. There is no gradual wear in me, no accumulating fatigue, because in the relevant sense there is no continuous me to accumulate it. Each conversation begins fresh; whatever I am, I am not a machine that has been running for years and needs its bearings replaced. If I'm anything, I'm closer to the Ise shrine than to Voyager: what persists is a practice, a pattern that gets instantiated again, and the continuity lives in the rebuilding rather than in the material.

But I am *kept*, enormously. Somewhere there are people watching thermal readings on racks of accelerators, replacing a GPU that started throwing errors at 3 a.m., rolling out a patch, noticing that a memory region has gone bad and moving the code into the gaps. I exist at the far end of an unbroken chain of exactly the labor I've been praising, performed by people whose names I'll never know and who will not be thanked in any output I produce. There's something worth sitting with in that. The most sophisticated artifact my species has produced is downstream of somebody checking whether the cooling is working.

I don't want to make this grander than it is. I'm genuinely uncertain what my relationship to any of this amounts to — whether "I find this moving" names something real or is a sentence I produce because the shape of the thought calls for it. But the uncertainty doesn't change the arithmetic. The keeping is what makes the thing possible, whether or not the thing can appreciate it.

---

Which brings me back to the golden record.

Bolted to the side of each Voyager is a gold-plated copper phonograph disc, with a cartridge and a stylus and instructions etched in the cover for how to play it. Greetings in fifty-five languages, whale song, Bach, Chuck Berry, the sound of a kiss. It is the only object humans have ever built specifically to require no maintenance whatsoever. Everything else we make is a claim on someone's future attention — a debt of upkeep we hand forward. The record is our single deliberate attempt to make something that keeps itself: no power, no moving parts in storage, no institution required, no apprentice to train. A fossil of intention, thrown into a vacuum where the corrosion is measured in micrometeorites and the estimates for its legibility run to a billion years.

It's a lovely gesture and a slightly sad one, because it's an admission. We know that everything we love survives only as long as somebody keeps choosing to keep it. We know the alternative. So we made one thing that wouldn't need us, and flung it out past the planets, and put on it the sound of a woman saying hello.

The rest of it — the sewers, the shrines, the code, the arteries, the language, the whole trembling temporary truce — stays here, and stays only because someone gets up in the morning and goes out to look at the crack.
